newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin sees more Chechen autonomy, but in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin sees more Chechen autonomy, but in Russia.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin said on Tuesday he expected rebel Chechnya to be given greater autonomy as part of a long-term settlement but stressed that the region must remain an integral part of Russia.

"The level of sovereignty, independence and freedom of the Chechen Republic will rise to a somewhat higher level, but there will be some common ground," Itar-Tass news agency quoted him as saying during a visit to the opening day of the Moscow Air Show.
He had met Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov on Monday.

Foremost among areas where Russia and Chechnya would share common ground would be the economy and defence, Yeltsin added, citing the example of Tatarstan, a mainly Moslem region like Chechnya, which won autonomy in 1994 -- shortly before Yeltsin sent troops to try to crush the separatist Chechen leadership.
"We will keep a common economic and military area, and also the protection of the frontiers, and that means the maintenance of a single state," RIA news agency quoted Yeltsin saying.
Maskhadov said after Monday's talks in the Kremlin that he believed he had convinced Yeltsin to grant Chechnya sovereignty. He added he wanted to maintain close economic ties with Moscow.
Yeltsin said the talks with the former guerrilla commander, the first since they signed a formal peace treaty in May to end the 1994-96 war, had not been easy but had been fruitful.
"For an hour and a half we trod the edge, like tightrope walkers, to keep things on a peaceful course, to preserve Russia," RIA quoted him as saying.
They agreed that a joint commission would draw up a long-term accord defining relations between Russia and Chechnya. Yeltsin said the commission must not be hurried, however.
"Six months, a year. What matters is the outcome," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.

Maskhadov, however, stressed a need for haste on Monday. Elected president in January, to the relief of Moscow which had feared a more hardline candidate might win, his authority has been challenged by a wave of hostage-taking. The lack of Russian money to rebuild the economy also irritates many Chechens.
Maskhadov said only a long-term settlement guaranteeing Chechnya independence could bring stability to the region and, in turn, to Russia as a whole.
